records.place: Villány, Villány wine district, southern Hungary

wine.name: Kopar Cuvée
wine.grapes: Cabernet Franc and Merlot lead, with a small share of Cabernet Sauvignon; until the 2006 vintage Cabernet Sauvignon led the blend.
wine.sites: Named for the Kopár vineyard on the southern slope of Szársomlyó between Villány and Nagyharsány, where the soil is so thin that the limestone shows; the house's notes for the 2022 also name Csillagvölgy, Konkoly and Ördögárok.
wine.making: Made only in the vintages the house judges strong enough. Since the 2018 vintage at least, the wine has aged for about sixteen months in small oak barrels, most of them new and the rest in their second use. The first vintage, 1997, spent eighteen months in new barriques, by the house's account, and the vineyards have been farmed organically since 2010.
wine.glass: Ripe plum and blackcurrant with black pepper, cigar box and toasted barrel spice, then cinnamon, graphite and tobacco as it opens; full and warm, with fine grained tannin. Older bottles turn to dried fruit and a savoury, tea like note.
wine.ageing: Firm in its first years; the house expects a strong vintage to keep for twenty years and more, and old bottles show dried fruit and a savoury edge.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The name of the Kopár vineyard; the word means barren, for its thin soil over limestone.
The protected wine district in the far south of Hungary, red country on a limestone ridge.
A blend of grapes, here Cabernet Franc, Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon.

records.table: Kopar is Gere's Villány blend, named for the bare limestone slope of Szársomlyó: Cabernet Franc and Merlot with a little Cabernet Sauvignon, aged in mostly new small oak. It is ripe and peppery, with plum and cigar box, and an hour in a decanter suits it.
records.story: The Gere family speaks of seven generations of winemaking in Villány, but its modern story begins with the end of communism. In 1992 the family bottled its first Phoenix Cuvée, a blend it has made every year since and named, as the house tells it, for the town's revival after the political change. In the same year it founded a joint winery in Villány with the Weninger family of Burgenland, bringing Austrian cellar technique south. Then came the wine that made the house's name. After a group of Villány growers travelled to Bordeaux, the family blended Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Cabernet Franc from its own sites with the 1997 vintage, aged it in new barriques and named it Kopar, after its vineyard: a fanciful name was itself new in Hungary in the 1990s. The 2000 vintage brought wide recognition. From 2006 the blend turned towards Cabernet Franc and Merlot, and from 2010 the vineyards were farmed organically. In 2024 Kopar joined the reference collection in the cellar of the Cité du Vin in Bordeaux. For a sommelier Kopar is the Villány Bordeaux blend in the house's own form: Cabernet Franc and Merlot from limestone, made only in the years the house judges strong enough.

wine.name: Bock Capella
wine.classification: Prémium, a tier of the Villány district's own classification above Classicus
wine.grapes: Cabernet Franc, the larger part, with Cabernet Sauvignon at about a third and a little Merlot.
wine.sites: Cabernet Franc from the Ördögárok vineyard and Cabernet Sauvignon from Jammertal, the family's historic vineyard, on limestone and loess.
wine.making: Made only in the years the house judges exceptional. The wine is fermented in vats and then aged for about two years in new barriques before bottling, and the house holds older vintages back for sale long after the harvest.
wine.glass: Dried plum, dark chocolate and tobacco over black cherry and sweet barrel spice; full and warm in alcohol, with dense, polished tannin from its long time in new oak.
wine.ageing: Built for the cellar after two years in new oak, it opens after about ten years and holds for a decade beyond in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: Latin for a chapel: the house cellar where it rests is built like one.
The protected wine district in the far south of Hungary.
The district's upper tier for oak aged reds, above Classicus, with lower yields.

records.table: Capella is Bock's selection, named for the chapel-like cellar where it rests: Cabernet Franc from Ördögárok with Cabernet Sauvignon from Jammertal, two years in new barriques, made only in exceptional years. It is ripe and dense, with dried plum and dark chocolate.
records.story: The Bock family counts nine generations of growers in Villány, and Jammertal, a vineyard famous in the district's history, has long been its own. In 1981, after his father's death, the founder of the modern estate made his first harvest on his own account, and by Magyar Bor's account the house first bottled its wine in 1987. When private estates returned after 1990 the family built quickly: in 1991 it made its first Bock Cuvée, the blend that has since carried the house's name, and the estate grew into one of the large private cellars of the district, with a hotel, the Ermitage, and a restaurant beside it. In 2006 Villány adopted its own tiers of quality, Classicus and Prémium, and Bock's oak aged blends sit in the upper one. Capella came as the house's own selection, a blend made only in the years it judges exceptional, named for the cellar built like a chapel where the wines rest; vintages such as 2006, 2007, 2009, 2011 and 2012 were made. In 2021 the house marked forty years since that first harvest. For a sommelier Capella shows the Villány idea at full weight: Cabernet Franc, limestone and long new oak.

Prémium is a tier of Villány's own classification, never a name the house chose for itself.

wine.name: Duennium
wine.grapes: A Bordeaux blend whose mix moves with the year: Merlot led the 2006, Cabernet Franc the 2015 and Cabernet Sauvignon the 2017, which carried a little Syrah.
wine.sites: Selected parcels of the estate's own vineyards on Fekete-hegy, the Black Hill above Kisharsány between Villány and Siklós, planted from 1992 onwards.
wine.making: Each variety is aged apart in 225 litre barrels of Hungarian oak, about half new and half a year old. After about seventeen months the cellar picks the lots with most character and blends them; in vintages such as 2012 and 2015 the blend then rests a further year in large wooden casks before bottling.
wine.glass: Dark forest fruits, dried plum and blueberry with cedar, cinnamon, clove and star anise, and dark chocolate in warm years; full, with velvety, ripe tannin and lively acidity.
wine.ageing: Made to keep: it gains savoury depth over ten years and more, and the house has offered its 2006 in magnum long after release.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The estate's name for its flagship blend, made only in the vintages it judges fit.

records.table: Duennium is Vylyan's flagship blend from the Black Hill above Kisharsány, made only in vintages the estate judges fit. Its lots age apart in Hungarian oak before the cellar blends the strongest, so it is full and velvety, with dried plum, cedar and clove.
records.story: By the estate's account Villány was Viliannak to the Romans and Vylyan in fifteenth century documents, and the founder chose that old name for his estate rather than his family's. He bought the base of the estate at Kisharsány in 1988, and from 1992 to 2004 the vineyards were planted on Fekete-hegy, the Black Hill between Villány and Siklós, with the winery built in the middle of the vines. The first bottled wine, a Kékoportó, followed in 1994, and the estate came to market in 1997. The founder died suddenly in 2004, and his widow took on the running of the estate. In 2008 Vylyan was named Winery of the Year in Hungary. Duennium is its answer to the Bordeaux blend: made only in the vintages the house judges fit, each variety aged apart in Hungarian oak and only the lots with most character blended. The 2012 won gold at a competition in Paris and won a Villány regional wine contest. For a sommelier Duennium is the wine of the district's younger estates, made by choice of lot rather than by a fixed recipe, so its grapes change from year to year.

Duennium ages in barrels of Hungarian oak, not French barriques; the estate names Zemplén and Mecsek oak for its 2006.

wine.name: Cuvée 7 Villány
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon leads, with Cabernet Franc and Merlot.
wine.sites: Three vineyards: Ördögárok, which gives the Cabernet Sauvignon at its base, and Kopár with its neighbour Konkoly on the southern face of Szársomlyó, where the wooded north side of the hill sends down cooling air.
wine.making: Fermented in stainless steel, then aged for about fifteen months in 225 litre French oak barrels, roughly a third of them new. The wine is then given about two years in bottle at the estate before it is released.
wine.glass: Cassis and blackcurrant with cedar, graphite and a little tobacco over sweet barrel spice; polished and full, with ripe, fine tannin and a long, warm finish.
wine.ageing: Released after its two years in bottle, it drinks well from then and gains cedar and savoury depth over the next five to ten years.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The estate's flagship blend; the label adds Villány or Siklós for two different wines.

records.table: Cuvée 7 Villány is Sauska's flagship, a Cabernet Sauvignon led blend from Ördögárok, Kopár and Konkoly, aged fifteen months in French oak and two years in bottle before release. It is polished and full, with cassis and cedar, and an hour of air suits it.
records.story: Sauska is a young house. By its own account a couple who had built a business abroad shared a dream of a family winery in Hungary, and it came true in Tokaj in 2003; the Villány estate followed, its first vintage in 2006. From the start the house built its Villány range on the Bordeaux grapes and on a few named sites under Szársomlyó: Kopár, which the estate calls the warmest vineyard in Hungary for its southern face, Konkoly beside it, cooled by the wooded north side of the hill, and Ördögárok. Cuvée 7 drew the three together and became the estate's flagship. Its 2007 vintage, from an estate barely two harvests old, won a regional trophy at the Decanter World Wine Awards, which brought the young house wide notice. Later the estate made a second Cuvée 7 from its sites at Siklós, in the west of the district, led by Merlot from the Makár vineyard on loess, so the label names which of the two is in the bottle. For a sommelier Cuvée 7 Villány shows the district's southern slopes through Cabernet Sauvignon, polished by French oak and long bottle ageing.

wine.name: Kúria Cabernet Franc
wine.sites: The Köves-föld vineyard at Máriagyűd, by Siklós in the west of the district; the name means stony ground.
wine.making: From organically farmed grapes, certified since 2009. The wine is matured in oak barrels and bottled without filtering, as every wine of the Kúria range is; by the estate's account its founder brought fermentation on fine lees and unfiltered bottling to the district.
wine.glass: Violet and blackberry with dark cherry, a leafy, grassy note of Cabernet Franc and sweet barrel spice; concentrated yet fresh, with fine, firm tannin and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Concentrated and oaky in youth, it is made to keep: the estate has offered vintages as old as 2002 and 2004 long after release.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

records.table: Malatinszky's Kúria Cabernet Franc is a single variety red from the stony Köves-föld vineyard at Máriagyűd, grown organically, aged in oak and bottled unfiltered. It is concentrated and fresh, with violet and blackberry, and should be decanted off any sediment.
records.story: By the estate's account the family's roots in wine lie in Badacsony, where landowning ancestors made wine in the eighteenth century. The modern estate is the work of a Budapest sommelier who left the restaurant Gundel in 1991 and soon opened a specialist wine shop in the capital. He began making his own wine in Villány in 1994, and in 1997 the winery was built and the estate set up again under the old name of a manor, a kúria. From the start the house set itself apart in the cellar: by its own account it brought fermentation on fine lees and unfiltered bottling to the district, and its Kúria range, above Signature and Noblesse, is bottled without filtering. In 2009 the estate turned to organic farming, and the Kúria wines carry organic certification. In the following years the district gave Cabernet Franc a designation of its own, Villányi Franc, and the grape became Villány's emblem. The Kúria Cabernet Franc, from the stony Köves-föld vineyard at Máriagyűd, had already shown the grape alone. For a sommelier it is a lesson in Villány Cabernet Franc without a blend to hide behind: concentrated, organic and unfiltered.
